QF.id: XIII Introduction to Forwards and Futures_60

question.text: What is the concept of 'cost of carry' being negative (inverse carry) and when does it occur?

answer.text: Negative cost of carry occurs when the income from holding the underlying (dividends for equity, coupon for bonds) exceeds the financing cost — resulting in futures trading below spot (backwardation)
Negative carry means the trader is losing money on their futures position
Negative carry is impossible — carry cost is always positive
Negative carry occurs only when interest rates are negative

explanation.text: The Logic: Net carry = financing cost minus income from holding the underlying. When income (dividends for equity, coupon for bonds) exceeds the financing cost, net carry turns negative and the fair futures price falls below spot, producing backwardation. A simple example is a high-dividend stock in a low-interest-rate environment. The Trap: Negative carry is not a loss on the futures position itself, it is a property of the carry model. It can arise without negative interest rates, and the concept applies to NET carry (income minus financing), not just to financing alone. Note: Replaced the truncated "F < S" expression with explicit "futures below spot/backwardation" wording so the formula text is readable; distributor/cross-exam framing removed.
